blocks.text: Introduction to Machine Learning built the map of the field, what learning even means, and which broad category a problem falls into. Data Collection and Understanding starts the real, practical work, because every one of those learning types needs actual data to learn from, and the shape that data comes in changes almost everything about how you handle it. Structured data is the natural place to begin, since it is the shape most machine learning courses, tools, and beginner projects are actually built around.

This topic goes through what structured data genuinely is, why the row and column shape matters so much for how a model actually consumes data, where this kind of data genuinely comes from in real systems, and a genuinely important caution, being structured is not the same thing as being correct.
1. What Structured Data Actually Is

blocks.alt: Rows and columns together make up a table

blocks.text: Structured data is information that already fits neatly into a predefined format of rows and columns, where every single row follows the exact same shape and every column has a clear, consistent meaning across the entire dataset. A spreadsheet of customer records is the clearest possible example, every row is one customer, every column is a specific, well defined attribute of that customer, an age, an income, a purchase history.

This rigid, predictable shape is exactly what makes structured data so easy to work with early on. A model, or even a simple query, can reliably assume that the age column always contains a number, and the purchased column always contains yes or no, because that structure was enforced when the data was originally collected or stored, typically in a relational database of the kind covered in the DBMS course on this platform.

blocks.text: 2. What a Row Genuinely Represents

blocks.alt: One row is one record representing one real entity

blocks.text: A row is a single, complete observation, and every value inside that row genuinely describes the exact same underlying thing. A row about one customer holds that customer age, that customer income, and that customer purchase history, all genuinely tied together, never mixed with values that actually belong to a different customer.

This might sound obvious, but it is precisely the property that makes a structured dataset trustworthy to work with, once you know a row genuinely represents one coherent thing, you can reason about that entire row as a single, real observation rather than a loose, disconnected bag of numbers.
3. What a Column Genuinely Represents

blocks.alt: One column is one attribute, holding the same type across every row

blocks.text: A column is a single, specific attribute measured consistently across every row. Every value in the age column genuinely represents an age, for a different observation each time, and every value in the income column genuinely represents an income, never accidentally something else entirely.

This consistency is what later lets you compute something like an average age across an entire dataset with genuine confidence that every number being averaged actually means the same thing, exactly the kind of computation the Statistical Summary topic later in this course relies on completely.
4. Where Structured Data Genuinely Comes From

blocks.alt: Databases, forms and logs, and sensors all produce structured data

blocks.text: Structured data typically comes from systems that were genuinely designed to enforce this rigid shape from the start. Relational databases are the most common real source, since a table in a database like PostgreSQL or MySQL genuinely cannot accept a row that violates its defined columns, the database itself rejects malformed data at write time.

Spreadsheets, exported CSV files, and structured logs from a well built application are other genuinely common sources. In every case, the structure exists because someone, or some system, deliberately imposed it, it is not an accident of how the data happened to be written down.

items: Relational databases, tables with a fixed, enforced schema.
Spreadsheets and exported CSV or Excel files.
Structured application logs with a consistent, predefined format.
Sensor readings recorded into a fixed set of numeric fields.

blocks.title: A useful mental test
blocks.content: If you can genuinely picture the data as a spreadsheet, with every row the same shape and every column meaning one consistent thing, you are almost certainly looking at structured data, regardless of which specific system it actually lives in.

blocks.text: 5. A Worked Example
A concrete table makes this genuinely concrete. A small structured dataset of house sales shows the row and column shape in practice, ready to be loaded directly into a model.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = {
    "square_feet": [1200, 1800, 950],
    "bedrooms": [2, 3, 1],
    "price": [250000, 400000, 180000],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)

blocks.text: Every row here is one house sale, every column is a consistent attribute measured the same way across all three rows. This is genuinely the exact shape that a regression model, covered in real depth later in this course, expects to receive as its training data.
6. Why This Shape Genuinely Matters for Machine Learning

blocks.alt: Consistent rows let a model read the data directly

blocks.text: Most classical machine learning algorithms, the regression and classification algorithms covered later in this course, genuinely expect data in this exact row and column shape, sometimes called tabular data, a specific term covered directly in its own topic next. A model cannot meaningfully learn from data with no consistent structure at all.

This is precisely why structured data is genuinely the easiest starting point for learning machine learning itself, the hard work of imposing consistent structure has already been done for you, letting you focus on the actual learning problem rather than first needing advanced techniques to extract structure from something genuinely messy.

blocks.text: 7. Structured Does Not Mean Correct

blocks.alt: A structured shape can still hide real errors

blocks.text: A structured, consistent shape does not automatically mean the actual values inside that shape are genuinely correct. A structured dataset can still have missing values, wrong types recorded, or genuinely bad data hiding inside a perfectly consistent shape, exactly the concerns covered in real depth in the Data Quality topic later in this module.

This distinction is genuinely worth holding onto throughout this entire course, structure is about the shape of the data, quality is about whether the actual values inside that shape can genuinely be trusted, and both matter, but they are not the same thing at all.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Structured data being easy to work with does not mean it is automatically clean or ready to use. A structured dataset can still have missing values, wrong types recorded, or genuinely bad data hiding inside a perfectly consistent shape, exactly the concerns covered in the Data Quality topic later in this module.

blocks.text: 8. Structured Data Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Structured data is covered first, unstructured data comes next

blocks.text: Structured data is genuinely the minority case in the real world, most of the data actually generated day to day, emails, images, audio, free form text, does not naturally arrive in this clean row and column shape at all. The next topic, Unstructured Data, covers exactly that other, genuinely more common case directly.

Understanding this specific contrast clearly, rigid and consistent versus genuinely free form, is the real foundation for everything else in this Data Collection and Understanding module, since nearly every later topic in this module, tabular data, time series data, data quality, ultimately traces back to this first, fundamental distinction.

items: Structured data fits a fixed, predefined shape of rows and consistent columns.
A row is one complete observation; a column is one consistent attribute measured across every row.
Relational databases, spreadsheets, and structured logs are common genuine sources of structured data.
Most classical machine learning algorithms expect data in this exact structured, tabular shape.
Being structured does not automatically mean the data is clean, missing values and bad entries can still hide inside it.
The next topic, Unstructured Data, covers the genuinely more common, free form alternative to this shape.
